1345.title: Newar Buddhism
1345.hook: in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley, a Sanskrit Buddhism with householder priests
1345.howItsDone: Newar Buddhists in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley worship at courtyard monasteries (bahas), with rituals in Sanskrit led by married, hereditary Vajracharya priests; boys of Vajracharya and Shakya families pass through a brief monastic ordination before returning to household life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many Nichiren communities, and a rule for hearing them all. Your line: each speaks for itself.

A narrow doorway off a busy street, and suddenly a courtyard. Pigeons on old paving stones. Laundry on a balcony. Children cutting across on their way to school. At the far end, a shrine, and in front of it a man in ordinary clothes, a husband and a father, ringing a small bell and reciting in Sanskrit. He's a priest. His family says his father was one too, and his father's father. The courtyard is still called a monastery, though families live along its edges. This is the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal.
screen: `A DOORWAY, THEN A COURTYARD.` → `A FATHER RINGING A BELL.` → `STILL CALLED A MONASTERY.`

segments.voice: First, who. The Newars are the people of the Kathmandu Valley, with their own language, their own cities and their own old crafts of metal, wood and painting. Some Newars are Buddhist, some Hindu, and in the valley the two share streets, festivals and sometimes the same holy places. Second, the language. Newar Buddhism is a Mahayana and Vajrayana tradition whose sacred texts and rituals are in Sanskrit. The valley's monasteries copied and recited Sanskrit Buddhist texts, and those texts are still read and honored in its temples. Third, the priests. Elsewhere on this path, the central figures were often monks who left home. Here the ritual heart belongs to householders. The Vajracharyas, whose name means vajra masters, are married priests who perform rites for families, and the Shakyas, whose name, tradition says, is the name of the Buddha's own clan, keep the shrines with them. A boy from these families goes through a monastic ordination rite, wears the robes for a short time, then returns to household life, carrying the monastery with him. Fourth, the courtyard and the festival. A baha or bahi is a courtyard monastery built around a shrine, with families living along its sides. And at festival time in the city of Patan, a towering chariot carrying Karunamaya, the compassionate one, is pulled through the streets by crowds, Buddhist and Hindu together. A religion that lives in a neighborhood, handed down at the dinner table as much as in the temple.
screen: `THE PEOPLE OF THE VALLEY.` · `SANSKRIT TEXTS AND RITES.` · `HOUSEHOLDER PRIESTS.` · `THE COURTYARD AND THE CHARIOT.` · then, large: `THE VALLEY'S WAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing your family has done for longer than you've been alive: a recipe, a song, a way of lighting a lamp or naming a child, and if an object tied to it is nearby, hold it in your hands. Picture the hands that did this before yours, one pair behind another, as far back as you can see. You don't have to keep the tradition to honor it; just let the line of hands be there with you, and breathe.
Newar Buddhism. The Buddhism of the Newar people of Nepal's Kathmandu Valley: Sanskrit texts, courtyard monasteries, and married householder priests. Today's word.
Your line: the valley's way. A monastery with families living in it. Rest well.

1346.title: The ten-day course
1346.hook: S. N. Goenka's ten-day silent courses in the method of U Ba Khin, offered on donations
1346.howItsDone: Students at S. N. Goenka's courses keep noble silence for ten days, practicing attention to the breath and then to sensations throughout the body; the courses charge no fee and are funded by donations from past students.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Newar Buddhism, where the priest at the shrine is also somebody's father. Your line: the valley's way.

At the front desk you hand over your phone. Your books go too, and your notebook, and your pen. Someone shows you to a simple room and a cushion in a quiet hall. For the next ten days you won't talk with the person on the next cushion, or catch their eye, or pass them a note. You'll sit, eat plain food, walk, sleep, and sit again. And at the end, nobody hands you a bill. People sign up for this, again and again.
screen: `HAND OVER THE PHONE.` → `NO TALKING, NO NOTES.` → `NO BILL AT THE END.`

segments.voice: First, the teachers. S. N. Goenka was born into an Indian family in Burma, now Myanmar, and became a businessman there. He learned meditation from U Ba Khin, a Burmese lay teacher who also served in his country's government. Goenka later began teaching in India, and the courses spread to centers around the world, taught in the same form in each place, with his recorded instructions guiding the students. Second, the silence. The courses ask for noble silence: no speaking, gestures or messages between students, so each person is left alone with their own mind. A student may still speak with the teacher about the practice, and with the staff about practical needs. Third, the method. It begins with the breath, attention resting on the small area around the nostrils, feeling the air come and go. When the mind has steadied, attention moves through the whole body, part by part: warmth, pressure, tingling, ache. The instruction is to observe without grasping the pleasant or pushing away the unpleasant, and to see that each sensation arises and passes. The Pali word for that passing is anicca, impermanence. On the final day comes metta, loving kindness, and the silence lifts. Goenka presented the method as belonging to no sect, something anyone could try without converting. Fourth, the money, or the lack of it. There's no charge for teaching, food or lodging. Courses run on donations from people who have finished one and want someone else to have the same chance. Every student sits, in a sense, as the guest of a stranger who came before.
screen: `FROM U BA KHIN TO GOENKA.` · `NOBLE SILENCE.` · `FIRST THE BREATH, THEN THE BODY.` · `OFFERED ON DONATIONS.` · then, large: `TEN DAYS OF SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Sit upright with your eyes closed, and rest attention on the small area just below the nostrils, above the upper lip, feeling the breath touch there, natural, as it is. When the mind wanders, come back without scolding yourself. Near the end, let attention move once, slowly, from the top of the head down to the toes, noticing whatever sensation is there and letting it pass.
The ten-day course. The silent meditation courses taught by S. N. Goenka in the method of U Ba Khin: breath, then body, offered free and funded by donations. Today's word.
Your line: ten days of silence. A gift from a stranger who sat before you. See you tomorrow.

1347.title: The insight movement
1347.hook: Western lay teachers who learned in Asia and teach vipassana at retreat centers
1347.howItsDone: In the insight movement, lay teachers lead vipassana and loving-kindness meditation at silent retreat centers and in weekly sitting groups, often using a soft noting of experience such as rising, falling, hearing and thinking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten-day course: silence, the breath, the body, and no bill at the end. Your line: ten days of silence.

Tuesday night, a rented room above a yoga studio. Folding chairs in a ring, cushions for anyone who wants the floor, coats piled by the door. The teacher wears a sweater, not a robe, and rings a small bell. A long silence. Then a short talk, about the breath, and about the day someone's mother died, and how to sit with that. A few questions. A laugh. At the end, everyone helps stack the chairs, and the room goes back to being a room. Nothing about it looks like a monastery.
screen: `A RENTED ROOM ON A TUESDAY.` → `A SWEATER, NOT A ROBE.` → `EVERYONE STACKS THE CHAIRS.`

segments.voice: Day nine fifty-one watched insight meditation go west; today, the movement it became. First, where it came from. A generation of young Americans and Europeans went to Asia to train: in Burma, in the lineage of Mahasi Sayadaw; in Thailand, with forest monks such as Ajahn Chah; in India, with teachers such as Anagarika Munindra and the householder teacher Dipa Ma. Some ordained for a time. Those who became teachers came home and taught as laypeople. Joseph Goldstein, Sharon Salzberg and Jack Kornfield are among the names. Together they helped found the Insight Meditation Society in Massachusetts, and Kornfield later helped found Spirit Rock in California. Second, what they teach. Vipassana is a Pali word usually translated insight, or seeing clearly. It rests on the Buddha's teaching on the setting up of mindfulness: watching the body, feelings, the mind and the things the mind knows, as they actually are. Some teachers use a gentle noting: silently naming rising, falling, hearing, thinking, then returning to the breath. Alongside it they teach metta, loving kindness, as a partner practice. Third, how it lives: silent retreats of a weekend or longer, and weekly sitting groups in rented rooms, living rooms and community halls. The teachers wear no robes; they teach people with jobs and families. Fourth, the questions. Teachers inside and outside the movement have asked honestly what is gained when meditation is taught apart from monasteries, ethics and devotion, and what might be lost, and the movement's own teachers have written about it too. Its aim stays plain: the clear seeing of the monastery, practiced in a kitchen, an office, a bus.
screen: `LAY TEACHERS WHO TRAINED IN ASIA.` · `VIPASSANA: SEEING CLEARLY.` · `RETREATS AND WEEKLY GROUPS.` · `HONEST QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `INSIGHT AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and find the breath where it's clearest, the belly or the chest. As it rises, note softly, rising; as it falls, falling; when a sound arrives, hearing, and when a thought pulls you away, thinking, and come back. No need to get it right: noticing is the practice.
The insight movement. Lay teachers who trained in Asia and came home to teach vipassana, insight meditation, at retreat centers and weekly groups. Today's word.
Your line: insight at home. No robe required, just a chair and a breath. I'll be here tomorrow.

1348.title: Won Buddhism
1348.hook: a Korean Buddhism of the twentieth century centered on a simple circle
1348.howItsDone: Won Buddhists enshrine the Il-Won-Sang, a plain circle, on their altars instead of a Buddha statue, meet for weekly services with meditation and chanting, and aim to practice anywhere and at any time, treating all things as a Buddha and every act as an offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the insight movement: lay teachers, rented rooms and vipassana, seeing clearly. Your line: insight at home.

On the altar there's no statue. No seated figure, no gold, no face. There's a circle: a plain black ring on a white field, framed and hung where a Buddha image might be. People bow to it, sit facing it in silence, and chant before it on a Sunday morning, in Seoul or in a converted house in an American suburb. A child in the back row might ask what it's a picture of. The answer takes a while.
screen: `NO STATUE ON THE ALTAR.` → `A PLAIN BLACK RING.` → `WHAT IS IT A PICTURE OF?`

segments.voice: First, the beginning. Won Buddhism is a modern Korean Buddhism. Its founder is known to his followers as Sotaesan. Tradition says he spent years searching for the truth without a teacher, questioning and struggling, until he awakened. Afterward he read the Buddhist scriptures, recognized his own awakening in the Buddha's teaching, and founded a new community. Won is the Korean word for circle. Second, the circle. It's called Il-Won-Sang, the One Circle image. Won Buddhists explain it as a symbol of the dharmakaya, the truth-body of the Buddha: the original nature of all beings and the source of everything. It isn't a picture of a person. It's a picture of what is already whole, before anyone draws a line through it, which is why it stands where a statue would. Third, what follows. If the one truth is everywhere, then, in a phrase Won Buddhists use, everywhere is a Buddha image, and every act is an offering to the Buddha. Your coworker, your child, the person in line at the pharmacy: each is a place to meet the Buddha. Work and family aren't interruptions of practice; they're where it happens. Won Buddhists speak of timeless Zen and placeless Zen: meditation that doesn't wait for the right hour or the right room. Fourth, the purpose. The founder's motto, in a paraphrase: as material civilization opens up, a spiritual civilization should open up with it. So Won Buddhism runs schools and charities alongside its temples, and its ministers, women and men alike, serve congregations that meet on ordinary weekends.
screen: `A MODERN KOREAN BUDDHISM.` · `IL-WON-SANG, THE ONE CIRCLE.` · `EVERYWHERE A BUDDHA IMAGE.` · `SPIRIT TO MATCH THE MATERIAL.` · then, large: `THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: If you have paper and a pen, draw one circle in a single motion, without lifting the pen, and don't fix it, even if it wobbles; with no paper, trace one slowly in the air. Rest your eyes on it: the inside, the outside, and the line between them. Let the breath go around with it, beginning and ending in the same place, and let it stand for a few moments for something whole.
Won Buddhism. A modern Korean Buddhism founded by Sotaesan, whose altar holds a plain circle, the One Circle image of the truth that is everywhere. Today's word.
Your line: the circle. Everywhere a Buddha image, and every act an offering. Until tomorrow.

1349.title: Triratna
1349.hook: a Western Buddhist community founded in 1967
1349.howItsDone: Members of the Triratna Buddhist Community go for refuge to the three jewels; those ordained into its order receive a new name and may be married or single, living in shared communities or alone, under the principle that commitment is primary and lifestyle secondary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Won Buddhism: a plain circle where a statue would stand, and every act an offering. Your line: the circle.

A woman walks into an ordination ceremony with the name her parents gave her, and walks out with a new one, a Sanskrit name her aunt will mispronounce at dinner for years. A simple stole now hangs around her neck for ceremonies. On Monday she'll be back at work as a nurse, and Monday night she'll cook for her kids. She hasn't become a nun. She has joined an order, and that difference sits near the heart of her community.
screen: `A NEW NAME AT ORDINATION.` → `BACK AT WORK ON MONDAY.` → `AN ORDER, NOT A CONVENT.`

segments.voice: First, the founder. Triratna was started in Britain by an Englishman known as Sangharakshita. Born Dennis Lingwood in London, he spent many years in India as a Buddhist monk, studying with teachers from several traditions. Back in Britain, he found people eager to practice and started a new community for them, which grew into what is now the Triratna Buddhist Community. Second, the name. Triratna is Sanskrit for the three jewels: the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, the community. Going for refuge to those three is at the center of the whole movement. Third, the big idea. Triratna has an order, and people are ordained into it with a new name. But the order is neither monks nor laypeople in the old sense. Its saying: commitment is primary, lifestyle secondary. A member may be married or single, may live in a shared house with other members or alone, may work an ordinary job or in one of the community's own businesses. What makes someone a member is going for refuge, not what they wear or where they sleep. The community draws freely on teachings from different Buddhist traditions, and on Western poetry and art too. Fourth, the hard part. A new community has no centuries of habit to steady it. Triratna has had to face painful accounts from former members about its founder's conduct and about harm in its early years, and it has published its own responses. Building something new means building, too, the ways to face what went wrong.
screen: `AN ENGLISH MONK BACK FROM INDIA.` · `THE THREE JEWELS.` · `COMMITMENT FIRST, LIFESTYLE SECOND.` · `FACING WHAT WENT WRONG.` · then, large: `NEW COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one community you know that's younger than you, or close to it: a congregation, a club, a support group, even a group chat. Ask quietly what holds its people together, not the logo or the rules but the thing they keep coming back for, and what it would need to admit, forgive and protect to stay healthy a long time, and breathe with those questions. If someone is hurting you or you're in danger, reach out: 988 in the US, or local emergency help.
Triratna. Sanskrit for the three jewels, and the name of a Western Buddhist community founded by Sangharakshita, whose order puts commitment before lifestyle. Today's word.
Your line: new community. Commitment first, lifestyle second, and honesty about the rest. See you tomorrow.

1350.title: Navayana
1350.hook: the "new vehicle" of Ambedkar's followers, centered on justice and equality
1350.howItsDone: Navayana Buddhists in India, including Dalit communities, take refuge in the Buddha, dharma and sangha, honor B. R. Ambedkar beside the Buddha, greet one another with Jai Bhim, and read the dharma as a call to equality and justice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Triratna: an order where commitment comes first and lifestyle second. Your line: new community.

Two people pass on a street in Maharashtra, and one says, Jai Bhim. The other says it back. It works as a hello, and it's also a name: Bhim, for Bhimrao Ambedkar. In homes and community halls, his picture hangs beside the Buddha's, often in a blue suit and glasses, holding a thick book against his chest. The book isn't a sutra. It's a constitution. A Buddhist shrine with a lawyer on it: that's where today begins.
screen: `JAI BHIM.` → `A PORTRAIT BESIDE THE BUDDHA.` → `A LAWYER HOLDING A CONSTITUTION.`

segments.voice: Day one thousand fifteen told of Ambedkar's conversion; today, the path that grew from it. First, the man. B. R. Ambedkar was born in India into a community the caste system treated as untouchable. As a child, he later wrote, he was made to sit apart at school and couldn't drink from the shared water. He became a lawyer and scholar, fought caste discrimination, and helped shape the constitution of independent India. Second, the choice. Ambedkar concluded that caste had no place in the path he wanted for his people, and after long study he chose the Buddha. At a great public ceremony in Nagpur, he took refuge in the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, then led a vast crowd of his followers through the same refuge, with vows that included rejecting caste and treating all people as equal. Third, the teaching. In The Buddha and His Dhamma, Ambedkar retold the Buddha's life and words with the weight on ethics and society: liberty, equality, fraternity, and the end of suffering in this life, between people. He read some traditional teachings in new ways. Some Buddhists elsewhere disagree with parts of his reading; his followers explain theirs in their own words. Navayana means the new vehicle, beside the older names for Buddhist paths. Fourth, today. For Dalit Buddhists, those the caste system pushed to the edges, Navayana can be a faith and a dignity at once. Temples hold the Buddha and Ambedkar side by side. And Jai Bhim is a greeting and, for those who say it, a promise: that the dharma has something to say about who sits where at school, who drinks from which cup, and who gets to be called a person.

1351.title: Secular Buddhism
1351.hook: practitioners who keep the practice and set aside rebirth and cosmology; others disagree; each explains itself
1351.howItsDone: Secular Buddhists practice meditation and the precepts and study the suttas while setting aside or holding open rebirth and traditional cosmology; teachers in traditional lineages answer that rebirth and karma are central to the Buddha's teaching, and both sides cite the Kalama Sutta.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navayana: the dharma read as equality. Your line: the new vehicle.

Can a person keep the cushion and set aside the cosmos? Sit every morning, keep the precepts, read the suttas closely, and still say, about rebirth and realms of gods and ghosts: I don't know, or I don't think so? Some practitioners say yes, and call themselves secular Buddhists. Others, teachers rooted in old lineages, say this cuts out something the Buddha himself put at the center. Both read the same texts. This week ends with a question, not a verdict.
screen: `KEEP THE CUSHION, SET ASIDE THE COSMOS?` → `SOME SAY YES.` → `OTHERS SAY NO.`

segments.voice: First, what secular Buddhists keep and set aside. They keep meditation, the precepts, the noble truths and the eightfold path, often read as things to do, not things to believe. They set aside, or hold open, rebirth, karma across lifetimes and the traditional map of heavens and hells. The writer Stephen Batchelor is one voice among them, and secular sanghas gather in person and online. Second, their case, in their words. They point to the Buddha's call to see for yourself, in the sutta to the Kalamas from day six fifty-seven: don't accept a teaching just because of tradition, report or a teacher's authority, but know for yourselves what leads to harm and what leads to good. They point, too, to the old phrase ehipassiko, come and see. Practice, they say, is what can be tested in this life. Third, the traditional reply. Teachers in Theravada, Tibetan and other lineages answer that rebirth and karma run all through the suttas. On the night of his awakening, the texts say, the Buddha saw his own past lives and the passing away and arising of beings according to their deeds. And nibbana, in those texts, is the end of rebirth itself. They note that the Kalama sutta goes on: the Buddha describes a person free of hatred who is at ease whether or not there is a world after this one. Both sides quote this sutta. Fourth, the week. A courtyard of householder priests, a silent course, lay teachers in rented rooms, a circle on an altar, a new order, a new vehicle, and now this. Each new form has had to answer the same question, what do we keep, and each explains its own answer.
screen: `KEEP THE PRACTICE, HOLD THE COSMOS OPEN.` · `THE SECULAR CASE: COME AND SEE.` · `THE TRADITIONAL REPLY: THE SUTTAS.` · `A WEEK OF NEW FORMS.` · then, large: `EACH EXPLAINS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a view on a big question that you don't share, and picture someone who holds it well, at their most thoughtful. Let them explain it in your mind, in their own words, all the way to the end, without arguing back; just breathe, listen, and notice what your body does. When they finish, thank them silently and let the picture go.
Secular Buddhism. Practitioners who keep meditation and ethics and set aside rebirth and traditional cosmology, while others in the tradition disagree. Today's word.
Your line: each explains itself. A question held open, heard from both sides. That's the week.
